# Systems and Hardware {#sec-appendix-systems}

This appendix supplies reference models for the timing, memory, communication, and electrical limits that connect learned proposals to physical actuators. Its derivations and worked estimates help readers calculate response budgets, interpret hardware measurements, and implement the record formats used by the permission path. Each model states assumptions that must hold before its result can support a physical operating limit.

## How to Use This Appendix

Consult this appendix when diagnosing physical systems bottlenecks, timing jitter, electrical rail instability, or hardware interface boundaries across chapters in this book:

| When you encounter this systems symptom                                                        | Consult                               | For this quantitative tool                                                                                             |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| Neural policy inference exhibits non-deterministic execution times or long latency tails       | @sec-appendix-systems-timers          | Execution-time analysis, static shape constraints, CUDA Graphs, and the limits of Extreme Value Theory (EVT) estimates |
| Real-time OS threads suffer latency spikes from page faults, cache bouncing, or IRQ preemption | @sec-appendix-systems-timers          | Memory locking (`mlockall`), stack prefaulting, 64-byte cache alignment, and top-half/threaded IRQ partitioning        |
| A software deadlock or kernel panic freezes actuator control loops                             | @sec-appendix-systems-timers          | Windowed watchdog detection, rolling polynomial token checkpoints, and Safe Torque Off (STO) response                  |
| Inverter bridge MOSFETs burn out or trip overcurrent protections                               | @sec-appendix-systems-inverters       | Microcontroller PWM complementary timers, dead-time insertion, Miller clamps, and 6th harmonic torque ripple           |

## Numbers to Know in Physical AI {#sec-appendix-systems-numbers-to-know}

```{python}
#| label: appendix-systems-numbers-to-know
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NUMBERS TO KNOW IN PHYSICAL AI (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appendix-systems-numbers-to-know, @tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy,
# │          @tbl-numbers-kinematics, @tbl-numbers-edge-compute, @tbl-numbers-thermal,
# │          @tbl-numbers-safety, and @tbl-numbers-buses.
# │ Goal: Centralize foundational orders of magnitude across rate hierarchies,
# │       kinetic stopping, edge memory streaming, thermal dynamics, statistical safety,
# │       and real-time fieldbuses.
# │ Show: Formatted physical reference figures sourced directly from mlsysim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_params,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    check,
    MarkdownStr,
)
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

class PhysicalNumbersToKnow:
    """Namespace for physical AI reference numbers, rate hierarchies, and scaling laws."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    R = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIRates
    K = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIKinematics
    T = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIThermal
    S = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAISafety
    B = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIBuses
    C = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAICompute

    # Rates
    intent_lo = R.IntentLo
    intent_hi = R.IntentHi
    chunk_lo = R.ChunkLo
    chunk_hi = R.ChunkHi
    permission = R.PermissionRate
    current_lo = R.CurrentLoopLo
    current_hi = R.CurrentLoopHi
    switching_lo = R.GateSwitchingLo
    switching_hi = R.GateSwitchingHi

    # Kinematics & Platforms
    _MPS = meter / second
    _MPS2 = meter / second**2
    hum_v = 1.0 * _MPS
    hum_a = 4.0 * _MPS2
    rm_v = 1.5 * _MPS
    rm_a = 2.0 * _MPS2
    bot_v = 6.0 * _MPS
    bot_a = 4.5 * _MPS2
    av_v = 30.0 * _MPS
    av_a = 7.0 * _MPS2

    tau_50 = 50 * millisecond
    tau_200 = 200 * millisecond

    # Compute & Memory
    vla_params_7b = C.VlaParameters7B
    vla_params_14b = 14e9 * param
    dram_bw = C.EdgeMemorySustainedOrin
    chunk_horizon = C.VlaChunkHorizon

    # Safety
    rule_of_three = S.RuleOfThreeMultiplier
    lambda_asild = S.TargetFailureRateASILD
    lambda_sil3 = S.TargetFailureRateSIL3
    lambda_robotaxi = 1e-6 / hour

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Rates & Periods
    intent_t_lo = (1 / intent_hi).to(millisecond)
    intent_t_hi = (1 / intent_lo).to(millisecond)
    chunk_t_lo = (1 / chunk_hi).to(millisecond)
    chunk_t_hi = (1 / chunk_lo).to(millisecond)
    perm_t = (1 / permission).to(millisecond)
    curr_t_lo = (1 / current_hi).to(microsecond)
    curr_t_hi = (1 / current_lo).to(microsecond)
    sw_t_lo = (1 / switching_hi).to(microsecond)
    sw_t_hi = (1 / switching_lo).to(microsecond)

    # Kinematics
    hum_blind_50 = (hum_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    hum_blind_200 = (hum_v * tau_200).to(millimeter)
    hum_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(hum_v, tau_200, hum_a).to(millimeter)
    hum_share_200 = (hum_blind_200 / hum_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    rm_blind_50 = (rm_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    rm_blind_200 = (rm_v * tau_200).to(millimeter)
    rm_stop_200_raw = calc_safe_stopping_distance(rm_v, tau_200, rm_a).to(millimeter)
    rm_stop_200 = float(Decimal(repr(rm_stop_200_raw.magnitude)).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)) * millimeter
    rm_share_200 = (rm_blind_200 / rm_stop_200_raw).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    bot_blind_50 = (bot_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    bot_blind_200 = (bot_v * tau_200).to(meter)
    bot_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(bot_v, tau_200, bot_a).to(meter)
    bot_share_200 = (bot_blind_200 / bot_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    av_blind_50 = (av_v * tau_50).to(meter)
    av_blind_200 = (av_v * tau_200).to(meter)
    av_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(av_v, tau_200, av_a).to(meter)
    av_share_200 = (av_blind_200 / av_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # Edge Compute (DRAM streaming time = Footprint / Sustained Bandwidth)
    fp16_bytes = 2 * byte / param
    int8_bytes = 1 * byte / param
    int4_bytes = 0.5 * byte / param

    footprint_7b_fp16 = (vla_params_7b * fp16_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_7b_int8 = (vla_params_7b * int8_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_7b_int4 = (vla_params_7b * int4_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_14b_int8 = (vla_params_14b * int8_bytes).to(GB)

    time_7b_fp16 = (footprint_7b_fp16 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_7b_int8 = (footprint_7b_int8 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_7b_int4 = (footprint_7b_int4 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_14b_int8 = (footprint_14b_int8 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)

    rate_single_7b_fp16 = (1 / time_7b_fp16).to(hertz)
    rate_single_7b_int8 = (1 / time_7b_int8).to(hertz)
    rate_single_7b_int4 = (1 / time_7b_int4).to(hertz)
    rate_single_14b_int8 = (1 / time_14b_int8).to(hertz)

    rate_chunk_7b_fp16 = rate_single_7b_fp16 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_7b_int8 = rate_single_7b_int8 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_7b_int4 = rate_single_7b_int4 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_14b_int8 = rate_single_14b_int8 * chunk_horizon

    # Safety bounds (N = 3 / lambda)
    hours_asild = (rule_of_three / lambda_asild).to(hour)
    hours_sil3 = (rule_of_three / lambda_sil3).to(hour)
    hours_robotaxi = (rule_of_three / lambda_robotaxi).to(hour)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(intent_hi < chunk_lo, "Intent band sits below chunk band.")
    check(chunk_hi < permission < current_lo, "Permission loop sits between chunk policy and current loop.")
    check(current_hi < switching_lo, "Current loop sits below inverter switching.")
    check(abs(perm_t.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "1 kHz has 1 ms period.")
    check(abs(time_7b_fp16.magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-3, "14 GB / 140 GB/s is 100 ms.")
    check(abs(time_7b_int8.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-3, "7 GB / 140 GB/s is 50 ms.")
    check(abs(time_7b_int4.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-3, "3.5 GB / 140 GB/s is 25 ms.")
    check(abs(hours_asild.magnitude - 3e8) < 1.0, "ASIL D hours: 3e8.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    intent_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(intent_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)}")
    chunk_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(chunk_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)}")
    perm_freq_str = fmt_frequency(permission, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    curr_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(current_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(current_hi, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)}")
    sw_freq_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt(switching_lo.to(ureg.kilohertz).magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(switching_hi, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)}"
    )

    intent_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(intent_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    chunk_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(chunk_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    perm_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(perm_t.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    curr_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(curr_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(curr_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µs")
    sw_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(sw_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(sw_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µs")

    intent_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(intent_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} mm")
    chunk_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(chunk_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} mm")
    perm_blind_str = fmt_length(1 * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    curr_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(curr_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(curr_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µm")
    sw_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(sw_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(sw_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µm")

    hum_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(hum_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(hum_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    rm_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(rm_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(rm_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    bot_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(bot_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(bot_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    av_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(av_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(av_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")

    hum_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(hum_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((hum_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    rm_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(rm_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((rm_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    bot_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(bot_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((bot_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    av_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(av_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((av_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )

    hum_blind_50_str = fmt_length(hum_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    hum_blind_200_str = fmt_length(hum_blind_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    hum_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(hum_stop_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)} ({fmt_percent(hum_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    rm_blind_50_str = fmt_length(rm_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    rm_blind_200_str = fmt_length(rm_blind_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    rm_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(rm_stop_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)} ({fmt_percent(rm_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    bot_blind_50_str = fmt_length(bot_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    bot_blind_200_str = fmt_length(bot_blind_200, unit=meter, precision=1)
    bot_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_length(bot_stop_200, unit=meter, precision=1)} ({fmt_percent(bot_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})")

    av_blind_50_str = fmt_length(av_blind_50, unit=meter, precision=1)
    av_blind_200_str = fmt_length(round(av_blind_200.to(meter).magnitude) * meter, unit=meter, precision=0)
    av_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(round(av_stop_200.to(meter).magnitude, 1) * meter, unit=meter, precision=1)} ({fmt_percent(av_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    fp_7b_fp16_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    fp_7b_int8_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)
    fp_7b_int4_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    fp_14b_int8_str = fmt_memory(footprint_14b_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)

    t_7b_fp16_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_fp16, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_7b_int8_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_int8, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_7b_int4_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_int4, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_14b_int8_str = fmt_latency(time_14b_int8, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    rate_s_7b_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_fp16, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_7b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_7b_int4_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_int4, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_14b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_14b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)

    rate_c_7b_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_fp16, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_7b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_7b_int4_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_int4, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_14b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_14b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    hours_asild_str = fmt(hours_asild.magnitude, precision=0, suffix=" hours")
    hours_sil3_str = fmt(hours_sil3.magnitude, precision=0, suffix=" hours")
    hours_robotaxi_str = fmt(hours_robotaxi.magnitude, precision=0, suffix=" hours")
```

Physical AI requires quantitative intuition across computation, motion, and heat. The latency hierarchy popularized by Jeff Dean[^fn-sys-jeff-dean] provides a useful starting point, but a delayed physical command also consumes clearance. The tables below separate representative rates and scenario calculations from bounds that require qualification on the actual machine.

The fastest events are transistor switching and local memory access. Operating-system dispatch and communication add scheduling and queueing delays. Actuator current then changes over an electrical time constant, while braking and heat accumulation unfold over longer intervals. These scales overlap; a task's assigned deadline comes from its physical consequence, not from its location in this hierarchy.

[^fn-sys-jeff-dean]: **Jeff Dean**\index{Dean, Jeff!latency numbers}: Google Senior Fellow and systems architect. His latency numbers originally presented with Peter Norvig around 2010 established the canonical latency hierarchy across storage, memory, and network tiers [@scott2012latency]. Physical AI extends this hierarchy down into electromechanical actuators, stopping kinematics, and thermal time constants.

::: {#psp-appendix-systems-three-numbers .callout-perspective title="Three physical numbers that matter most"}

* **Kinetic equivalence: $1\text{ ms} = 1\text{ mm}$ (at $1\text{ m/s}$)**: At a nominal robotic speed of $1\text{ m/s}$, every single millisecond of perception, inference, or fieldbus latency translates into exactly $1\text{ mm}$ of blind travel before retarding torque can be applied. At highway velocity ($30\text{ m/s}$), each millisecond is $3\text{ cm}$. In physical systems, software latency is not waiting time; it is physical displacement.
* **Thermal divergence: $\tau_{\text{silicon}} \sim 1\text{ ms}$ vs. $\tau_{\text{stator}} \sim 100\text{ s}$**: Semiconductor junctions heat adiabatically within milliseconds during deep neural network bursts, potentially triggering thermal throttling before heat spreaders react. Electrical rail droop is a separate response to changing current demand. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over tens to hundreds of seconds, tolerating transient overcurrent for aggressive maneuvers but accumulating thermal energy that eventually limits sustained torque.
* **The exposure wall: $N = 3 / \lambda$**: Under a stationary Poisson model, zero observed failures gives an approximate one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound of $3/N$ after $N$ operational hours [@hanley1983nothing]. Very small target rates demand correspondingly large exposure. Runtime barriers can support a broader assurance argument, but neither a barrier nor a finite test proves the absence of failure.

:::

### Rate and latency hierarchy across machine levels

Control rates in physical AI rise steeply from the deliberative brain down to the physical body (@tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy). Deliberative multimodal models (VLAs) operate at human reaction scales ($1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$). Action chunking models emit future trajectory waypoints at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. Beneath the proposal boundary, the permission path enforces safety barriers at $1\text{ kHz}$. At the lowest levels, power electronic current loops and PWM switching operate at tens to hundreds of kilohertz to maintain electromagnetic flux and drive torque. For real-time timer schedulability and response-time analysis, see @sec-appendix-systems-timers; for inverter gate switching and dead-time modeling, see @sec-appendix-systems-inverters.

| Machine Level                   | Frequency Band                                   | Cycle Period                                       | Blind Travel at 1 m/s                             | Architectural Mechanism & Bound                                                   |
|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Brain (Deliberation)**        | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_freq_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_period_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_blind_str` | Multimodal VLA reasoning; memory- and compute-bound                               |
| **Brain (Action Chunking)**     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_freq_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_period_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_blind_str`  | Action chunk diffusion/transformer decoding; amortized                            |
| **Nervous System (Permission)** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_freq_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_period_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_blind_str`   | Control barrier certificates, stopping envelopes, lease watchdog                  |
| **Body (Current Loop)**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_freq_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_period_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_blind_str`   | Field-oriented current control (FOC), torque tracking, stator flux                |
| **Body (Inverter Switching)**   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_freq_str`     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_period_str`     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_blind_str`     | Power MOSFET gate drive, dead-time insertion ($t_{\text{dead}}$), inductive droop |

: **Rate and Latency Hierarchy Across the Five Machine Levels**: Representative rates from inverter switching to foundation-model deliberation. The reciprocal period and travel during that period at nominal speed ($1\text{ m/s}$) are scale comparisons, not independently established deadlines or evidence-age bounds. {#tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[18,16,16,18,32]"}

### Kinetic translation and safe stopping envelopes

Total stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2 / (2 a_{\text{brake}})$ combines the linear blind travel accrued during computational delay and the quadratic mechanical braking distance (@tbl-numbers-kinematics). As platform speed increases, absolute blind travel expands rapidly, consuming entire clearance margins before deceleration can begin. @Sec-appendix-systems-stopping derives the information-age and braking terms; @sec-appendix-systems-rotor-jerk relates joint jerk to electrical limits.

| Platform Archetype               | Nominal Velocity $v$                       | Braking Decel $a$                          | Blind Travel ($\tau=50\text{ ms}$)                | Blind Travel ($\tau=200\text{ ms}$)                | Total Stop ($\tau=200\text{ ms}$)                 |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| **Humanoid / Quadruped**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_v_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_a_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_blind_50_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_blind_200_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_stop_200_str` |
| **Warehouse Mobile Manipulator** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_v_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_a_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_blind_50_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_blind_200_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_stop_200_str`  |
| **Urban Delivery Robot**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_v_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_a_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_blind_50_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_blind_200_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_stop_200_str` |
| **Autonomous Vehicle (Highway)** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_v_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_a_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_blind_50_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_blind_200_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_stop_200_str`  |

: **Kinetic Translation Across Platform Archetypes**: Pre-brake delay converts into unrecoverable physical travel before braking force begins. These illustrative archetypes assume constant speed during delay and constant braking afterward; they are not the running machine's qualified profiles. Parenthesized percentages give blind travel as a share of the modeled total. {#tbl-numbers-kinematics tbl-colwidths="[20,16,16,16,16,16]"}

### Edge memory bandwidth and action chunk amortization {#sec-appendix-systems-memory-bound}

For $O$ operations and $D_{\text{vol}}$ bytes transferred from memory, an idealized execution-time lower bound is $\max(O/R_{\text{peak}},D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW})$, where $R_{\text{peak}}$ is peak arithmetic throughput and $\text{BW}$ is available memory bandwidth. The equivalent roofline throughput bound is $\min(R_{\text{peak}},(O/D_{\text{vol}})\text{BW})$. The ratio $O/D_{\text{vol}}$ is arithmetic intensity. This model identifies whether compute or memory transfer binds; synchronization, contention, and incomplete overlap increase actual time.

At small batch sizes, autoregressive generation can be limited by memory bandwidth. @Tbl-numbers-edge-compute divides weight storage by the assumed sustained bandwidth to obtain a streaming-only lower bound on execution time. A chunk decoder that produces all $H$ waypoints in one weight pass can amortize that transfer; one that makes multiple denoising or token-generation passes cannot claim the same amortization. The resulting waypoint rate is an output-throughput ceiling, not a fresh-observation feedback rate. @Sec-appendix-systems-dram explains how competing traffic reduces the bandwidth available to the decoder.

### Thermal time constants across compute and electromechanics

For a constant heat input and a single thermal node initially at ambient, temperature follows $T(t) = T_{\text{amb}} + \Delta T_{\max} (1 - e^{-t/\tau_{\text{th}}})$ with steady-state rise $\Delta T_{\max}$ and time constant $\tau_{\text{th}}$ (@tbl-numbers-thermal). Local silicon temperature can change rapidly during a computational burst, requiring thermal qualification of the workload and cooling path. Electrical droop has a separate current-transient timescale. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over minutes, allowing transient torque overdrive if bounded by an $I^2 t$ thermal watchdog. For first-order thermal differential equations and stator winding degradation limits, see @sec-appendix-systems-actuators; for regenerative energy absorption on DC power buses, see @sec-appendix-systems-power.

| Subsystem Component         | Physical Mechanism                       | Thermal Time Constant $\tau_{\text{th}}$ | Critical Failure Mode                                     | Safety Mitigation                            |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| **Silicon Junction (Die)**  | Transistor channel self-heating          | 1–10 ms                                  | Gate delay change, leakage rise, thermal trip             | Thermal monitoring and frequency throttling  |
| **SoC Heat Sink / Package** | Convective heat spreader dissipation     | 10–60 s                                  | Package thermal saturation, sustained throttling          | Active fan modulation, workload migration    |
| **Motor Stator Windings**   | Copper resistive Joule heating ($I^2 R$) | 30–180 s                                 | Insulation breakdown (Class H $180^\circ\text{C}$), short | $I^2 t$ thermal protection, current derating |
| **Motor Frame / Housing**   | Bulk metallic casing heat conduction     | 10–30 min                                | Structural deformation, bearing grease loss               | Natural convection, passive cooling fins     |
| **Traction Battery Pack**   | Electrochemical cell internal resistance | 5–20 min                                 | Chemistry-dependent overheating and thermal runaway       | Liquid cooling loop, charge/discharge cutoff |

: **Thermal Time Constants Across Compute and Electromechanical Subsystems**: Thermal response spans several orders of magnitude. The listed ranges are representative scales, not universal device limits. Heating rates, thermal trips, and sustained torque require the actual thermal network and initial temperature. {#tbl-numbers-thermal tbl-colwidths="[20,18,16,22,24]"}

### Statistical safety bounds and exposure walls

For zero observed failures in stationary Poisson exposure, the one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound is approximately $3/N$, where $N$ is total operating time [@hanley1983nothing]. @Tbl-numbers-safety shows the exposure needed to put that bound at three illustrative target rates. These are statistical calculations, not a mapping from a whole-system accident rate to a safety integrity level. In particular, ISO 26262 random-hardware-failure metrics do not describe every cause of a learned system's failure [@iso26262]. Correlated trials, changing operating conditions, and unobserved failures invalidate a naive accumulation of hours.

| Illustrative target rate $\lambda$ | Required failure-free exposure $N \approx 3/\lambda$ | Interpretation                                          |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| $10^{-8}/\text{hour}$              | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hours_asild_str`     | Upper rate bound under the declared Poisson model       |
| $10^{-7}/\text{hour}$              | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hours_sil3_str`      | Same confidence level and observation assumptions       |
| $10^{-6}/\text{hour}$              | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hours_robotaxi_str`  | A rate alone does not establish a safety classification |

: **Statistical Testing Exposure**: Approximate exposure for a one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound after zero observed failures. A system assurance argument also needs evidence about failure mechanisms and operating conditions. {#tbl-numbers-safety tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

### Fieldbus latencies, jitter, and determinism

Communication buses exhibit sharp divides in latency and jitter (@tbl-numbers-buses). Whereas distributed cluster fabrics (such as RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) prioritize aggregate bandwidth using credit-based flow control and statistical multiplexing, onboard physical AI buses must guarantee bounded delivery times. Industrial fieldbuses such as EtherCAT combine hardware forwarding with scheduled exchange and clock synchronization; a specific jitter claim requires the configured system's evidence. Classical serial buses like CAN 2.0B provide low-overhead bitwise arbitration for up to 8 bytes, but saturate rapidly under multi-joint control traffic; CAN-FD expands payloads to 64 bytes with accelerated data bit rates. Meanwhile, switched IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) uses scheduled transmission gates to multiplex gigabit vision streams with hard real-time actuator commands. In contrast, non-deterministic best-effort Ethernet and shared wireless channels introduce tail latencies that exceed the reaction deadlines of high-speed electromechanical machines. For IEEE 1588 PTP hardware timestamping bounds, see @sec-appendix-systems-ptp; for CAN 2.0B vs. CAN-FD priority arbitration and EtherCAT cycle budgets, see @sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus.

| Bus / Network Technology       | Nominal Transit Latency                | Illustrative Jitter                  | Determinism Mechanism                               | Primary Machine Role                                                |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **EtherCAT (ETG.1000)**        | $100\,\mu\text{s}\text{--}1\text{ ms}$ | $< 1\,\mu\text{s}$                   | Hardware cut-through on-the-fly frame processing    | Synchronous joint servo drive & sensor feedback (Body/Nervous)      |
| **CAN-FD (ISO 11898-1)**       | $100\text{--}500\,\mu\text{s}$         | $50\text{--}200\,\mu\text{s}$        | Bitwise non-destructive priority arbitration (64 B) | Distributed sensors, multi-axis actuator controllers (Nervous/Body) |
| **CAN 2.0B (ISO 11898-1)**     | $200\,\mu\text{s}\text{--}1\text{ ms}$ | $100\text{--}400\,\mu\text{s}$       | Bitwise non-destructive priority arbitration (8 B)  | Legacy sensors, low-rate auxiliary controllers (Nervous/Body)       |
| **TSN Ethernet (802.1Qbv)**    | $10\text{--}100\,\mu\text{s}$          | $< 5\,\mu\text{s}$                   | Time-aware shaper with scheduled transmission gates | High-bandwidth sensor ingress (lidar/cameras) to SoC (Boundary)     |
| **Standard IP / UDP Ethernet** | $0.5\text{--}5\text{ ms}$              | $1\text{--}20\text{ ms}$             | Switched full-duplex links; best-effort queueing    | Asynchronous logging, inter-node telemetry (Brain)                  |
| **Shared Wi-Fi telemetry**     | $5\text{--}20\text{ ms}$               | $10\text{--}500\text{ ms}$ (RF fade) | Wireless packet retransmission, contention window   | High-level fleet dispatch, cloud mission updates (World/Governance) |

: **Communication Bus Latencies, Jitter, and Real-Time Determinism**: Representative scales for configured networks, not protocol-level worst-case guarantees. Required jitter follows the plant and deadline; bounded control does not universally require sub-microsecond jitter. Delivery guarantees require a traffic model, topology, arbitration analysis, and measured implementation behavior. {#tbl-numbers-buses tbl-colwidths="[18,16,16,22,28]"}

## Real-Time Timers, Watchdogs, and Schedulability {#sec-appendix-systems-timers}

A real-time task is correct only if it computes the required result before its deadline. Average inference latency and throughput do not establish that property. A permission task needs a bound that includes its own execution, blocking on shared resources, and interference from other work.

The following single-core scheduling models separate those contributions. Their guarantees apply only under their stated task assumptions; operating-system configuration and loaded measurements must establish whether the implementation satisfies them.

### Real-time task schedulability under rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first scheduling

In contrast to general-purpose Linux time-sharing, real-time operating systems schedule tasks based on deterministic timing contracts rather than dynamic heuristics. A periodic real-time task $\tau_i$ is characterized by its worst-case execution time (WCET) $C_i$, relative deadline $D_i$, and period $T_i$.\index{Real-time systems!worst-case execution time}\index{Rate-Monotonic Scheduling!utilization bound}\index{Earliest Deadline First!dynamic scheduling}\index{Linux kernel!SCHED_DEADLINE} When multiple real-time tasks share a single core, schedulability depends on the priority assignment discipline:

**Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS).** Fixed-priority preemptive scheduling where priority is assigned inversely proportional to task period ($T_i < T_j \implies \text{priority}(\tau_i) > \text{priority}(\tau_j)$) [@liu1973scheduling]. For a set of $n$ independent periodic tasks, with negligible scheduling overhead, no blocking or release jitter, and implicit deadlines ($D_i = T_i$), a sufficient condition for schedulability is the Liu and Layland utilization bound:
$$ U = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{C_i}{T_i} \le n \left( 2^{1/n} - 1 \right) $$
As $n \to \infty$, the bound converges monotonically to $\lim_{n \to \infty} n(2^{1/n}-1) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ (69.3 percent). If total processor utilization does not exceed 69.3 percent, the task set is guaranteed to meet all deadlines under RMS. When task periods form a harmonic set—where every period is an exact integer multiple of every shorter period ($T_j = k \cdot T_i$ for integer $k \ge 1$, such as $1\text{ ms}$, $5\text{ ms}$, $10\text{ ms}$, and $100\text{ ms}$)—the utilization bound rises to 100 percent. In physical AI architectures, rate hierarchies are purposefully engineered with harmonic cadences to maximize processor utilization without sacrificing determinism.

**Response Time Analysis (RTA).** When processor utilization exceeds the conservative Liu and Layland bound ($U > \ln 2$), or when relative deadlines are constrained ($D_i \le T_i$), exact schedulability requires evaluating the worst-case **response time** $R_i$ [@liu1973scheduling; @kopetz2011real]:
$$ R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i $$
where $B_i$ is the maximum blocking duration induced by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources, and $I_i$ is the interference from higher-priority tasks. The response time is computed via the fixed-point recurrence:
$$ R_i^{(k+1)} = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i^{(k)}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j $$
For fixed priorities, bounded blocking, no self-suspension, and zero release jitter, start with $R_i^{(0)} = C_i + B_i$ and iterate until $R_i^{(k+1)} = R_i^{(k)} \le D_i$ (establishing schedulability) or $R_i^{(k+1)} > D_i$ (signaling deadline violation). See @sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis and @sec-nervous-rta-variance for the role of response time variance in the nervous system.

**Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and `SCHED_DEADLINE`.** In dynamic-priority systems, EDF assigns highest priority to the active task with the closest absolute deadline $d_{i,k} = r_{i,k} + D_i$. For independent jobs on a single-core preemptive processor with no blocking and negligible scheduling overhead, EDF is optimal: if a task set is schedulable by any scheduling algorithm, it is schedulable by EDF [@liu1973scheduling]. For periodic tasks with $D_i = T_i$, EDF guarantees schedulability if and only if:
$$ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{C_i}{T_i} \le 1 $$
achieving 100 percent theoretical utilization without requiring harmonic periods. When relative deadlines are strictly less than periods ($D_i < T_i$), schedulability requires the processor demand criterion over the Demand Bound Function (DBF):
$$ \text{dbf}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \max\left( 0, \left\lfloor \frac{t - D_i}{T_i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) C_i \le t, \quad \forall t \ge 0 $$
evaluating whether cumulative execution demand exceeds available physical time across all time intervals $t$. Under Linux, EDF is exposed via the `SCHED_DEADLINE` policy implementing the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) algorithm. A CBS task declares its runtime $Q_i$, deadline $D_i$, and period $P_i$ via `sched_setattr()`. If a task attempts to execute beyond its declared runtime $Q_i$ within period $P_i$, the kernel dynamically throttles the task until its next period, protecting co-located real-time threads from execution overruns.

**Priority Inversion and Resource Sharing.** In standard multi-threaded Linux, mutual exclusion primitives (such as futex-backed mutexes) assume threads will eventually yield the processor. When real-time tasks share data structures (such as seqlock mailboxes or actuator command queues) protected by naive mutual exclusion, they suffer from **unbounded priority inversion** [@sha1990priority; @reeves1997pathfinder]. A low-priority task $\tau_L$ acquires a lock; a high-priority task $\tau_H$ becomes ready and blocks waiting for the lock; intermediate-priority tasks $\tau_M$ that do not need the lock preempt $\tau_L$, delaying $\tau_H$ for an arbitrary duration.

To bound blocking time $B_i$ in the RTA recurrence, real-time operating systems employ formal synchronization protocols:

1. **Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP)**: When $\tau_H$ blocks on a lock held by $\tau_L$, the operating system temporarily elevates $\tau_L$'s active priority to $\tau_H$'s priority, preventing preemption by $\tau_M$. Under `PREEMPT_RT` Linux, standard in-kernel spinlocks are converted to sleeping `rt_mutex` locks that enforce PIP automatically, while user-space threads configure `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`. While PIP eliminates unbounded inversion, it permits transitive blocking chains ($B_i \le \sum_{k} C_k$) and potential deadlock.
2. **Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP)**: Each lock is assigned a static priority ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it. A task $\tau_i$ can lock a resource only if its priority is strictly higher than the priority ceilings of all locks currently held by other tasks. PCP prevents mutual-exclusion deadlocks and guarantees that a task is blocked at most once by at most one lower-priority critical section [@sha1990priority]:
$$ B_i = \max_{k \in lp(i), s \in cs(k)} C_{k,s} $$
where $lp(i)$ is the set of tasks with priority lower than $\tau_i$, and $cs(k)$ is the set of critical sections executed by task $\tau_k$ with a priority ceiling at or above the priority of $\tau_i$.

### Worst-case execution time analysis for physical ML pipelines

In classical embedded systems, the worst-case execution time $C_i$ is determined via Static Timing Analysis (STA) [@hennessy2019computer]. STA parses binary machine instructions, constructs a Control Flow Graph (CFG), and solves an Integer Linear Program via the Implicit Path Enumeration Technique (IPET) using cycle-accurate microarchitectural models of processor pipelines, branch predictors, and cache sets.

In physical AI systems, evaluating $C_i$ for learned vision-language-action (VLA) and diffusion policies presents distinct architectural challenges:\index{Physical AI!WCET analysis}\index{Extreme Value Theory!execution time tail bounds}\index{CUDA Graphs!deterministic kernel dispatch}

1. **Microarchitectural opacity**: Modern neural accelerators (GPUs, NPUs, Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) hardware) feature multi-level shared caches, dynamic frequency scaling (DVFS), out-of-order warp schedulers, and memory crossbar contention that make a sound static bound difficult without detailed timing and interference models.
2. **Algorithmic execution variance**: Learned pipelines exhibit dynamic execution paths, including adaptive denoising loops in diffusion models, variable sequence lengths in autoregressive decoders, and data-dependent sparse attention kernels.
3. **Software runtime overhead**: Deep learning runtimes (e.g., PyTorch, TensorRT, Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime) introduce non-deterministic host-to-device kernel launch queueing, unified memory migration, and internal memory allocation locks. Launch overhead and jitter depend on the runtime, driver, submission path, and load; a per-kernel constant is not portable across systems.

To constrain execution variability for neural policies that cross the proposal boundary, physical AI systems enforce deterministic execution contracts and hybrid measurement bounds:

* **Static shape contracts**: Action chunk horizons ($H$), token context lengths, and sensor input tensors are locked to fixed maximum dimensions. Dynamic input padding replaces variable-length tensors, ensuring constant compute graph geometry and eliminating dynamic kernel recompilation.
* **Zero runtime allocation**: All execution buffers, KV caches, scratchpad memory, and direct memory access (DMA) descriptors are preallocated during initialization. Dynamic memory calls (`malloc`, `cudaMalloc`, `free`) are strictly forbidden on cyclic control paths.
* **Reduced host dispatch overhead via CUDA Graphs**: Fixing denoising iterations bounds one source of algorithmic work. Capturing and instantiating a reusable graph reduces repeated per-kernel host setup, as the [CUDA Graphs documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/cuda-graphs.html) explains. Graph launch still uses the runtime and driver, and device scheduling, frequency changes, and shared-resource contention remain. A graph does not by itself provide deterministic execution.
* **Extreme Value Theory (EVT) tail bounds**: Because finite empirical profiling cannot expose the true maximum execution time under worst-case hardware interference, engineers apply Extreme Value Theory [@coles2001introduction]. Under the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem, execution time exceedances over a high operational threshold $u$ converge asymptotically to a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD):
$$ G(y) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\tilde{\sigma}} \right)^{-1/\xi} $$
on the support $1+\xi y/\tilde{\sigma}>0$, with the exponential limit at $\xi=0$. Here $y = x - u > 0$, $\tilde{\sigma} > 0$ is the scale parameter, and $\xi$ is the shape parameter (tail index). The shape parameter characterizes the tail behavior:

  - $\xi < 0$ (Weibull domain): Bounded upper tail with a finite model endpoint $x_{\max} = u - \tilde{\sigma}/\xi$, under the fitted model; an estimated finite endpoint is not proof of a hardware ceiling.
  - $\xi = 0$ (Gumbel domain): Light, exponential tail.
  - $\xi > 0$ (Fréchet domain): Heavy, polynomial tail. The fitted sign alone neither identifies a hardware failure mechanism nor determines whether a deadline can be defended.

For an acceptable target exceedance probability $\epsilon$ (such as $10^{-6}$ or $10^{-8}$ per invocation), a model-based execution-time quantile $C_{\text{tail}}(\epsilon)$ is computed as:
$$ C_{\text{tail}}(\epsilon) = u + \frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{\xi} \left[ \left( \frac{N}{N_u} \epsilon \right)^{-\xi} - 1 \right] $$
where $N$ is total sample count and $N_u$ is the count of observations exceeding threshold $u$. For $\xi=0$, the continuous limit is $u-\tilde{\sigma}\ln(N\epsilon/N_u)$. These are fitted quantiles, conditional on the sampling regime, threshold choice, tail model, and parameter uncertainty. They do not certify a deterministic WCET. A placement ledger must distinguish measured maxima, probabilistic estimates, and justified execution bounds; the permission path must remain schedulable when the proposer exceeds its estimate.

### Operating-system determinism through interrupt handling, memory locking, and cache locality

On a heterogeneous robotics system on chip (SoC), the nervous system and safety monitors execute under real-time operating systems (RTOS) or real-time Linux kernels (such as Linux patched with `PREEMPT_RT`).\index{Real-time operating system!interrupt latency}\index{Memory locking!mlockall page fault elimination}\index{Real-time Linux!kernel mechanics}\index{Linux kernel!CFS vs SCHED_FIFO}\index{CPU isolation!nohz_full and isolcpus}\index{Cache locality!false sharing and 64-byte alignment} Interrupts and non-preemptible kernel critical sections can delay user-space tasks; a hard response bound requires bounding those intervals on the chosen kernel and hardware. In physical AI pipelines where control loops govern physical momentum, operating-system determinism requires eliminating non-preemptible kernel sections, bounding interrupt preemption latency, isolating execution cores, locking virtual memory, and enforcing cache locality.

**Fair Scheduling vs. Real-Time Policies.** Linux fair scheduling balances CPU service among runnable tasks. Its historical CFS implementation accounts for weighted execution time; newer kernels use [EEVDF](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html), which also considers eligibility and virtual deadlines. Neither policy establishes the physical deadline guarantee needed by the permission task.

In physical AI systems, real-time control threads must instead be configured with POSIX static priority scheduling policies (`SCHED_FIFO` or `SCHED_RR`) across priority levels 1 to 99 (or `SCHED_DEADLINE` implementing Earliest Deadline First). Under `SCHED_FIFO`, the highest-priority runnable thread executes immediately and runs until it blocks on I/O, yields voluntarily, or is preempted by a strictly higher-priority real-time thread.

**PREEMPT_RT Kernel Architecture.** In mainline Linux kernels, disabling preemption during spinlock acquisition (`preempt_disable()`), executing non-preemptible softirqs, and servicing asynchronous workqueues can delay user-space execution by tens of milliseconds. When an unprivileged machine learning process or device driver holds an in-kernel spinlock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time safety task cannot preempt the CPU, even if its timer has expired. A kernel configured with `PREEMPT_RT` reduces non-preemptible execution through the mechanisms below. Hardware, drivers, and remaining critical sections still require timing qualification.

1. *Sleeping Spinlocks (`rt_mutex`)*: Standard in-kernel spinlocks (`spinlock_t` and `rwlock_t`) are replaced by sleeping mutexes backed by `rt_mutex` with Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) support. When a high-priority thread waits for an `rt_mutex`, the waiter sleeps and the lock owner inherits its priority until it can release the lock. Raw spinlocks remain non-preemptible; interrupt masking depends on the primitive used. Their maximum hold times must be included in the platform timing analysis.
2. *Preemptible Read-Copy Update (`CONFIG_PREEMPT_RCU`)*: RCU read-side critical sections (`rcu_read_lock()` / `rcu_read_unlock()`) become preemptible, preventing deferred memory reclamation from stalling real-time threads.
3. *Forced Interrupt Threading*: Hardware interrupt service routines (ISRs) are split into minimal top-half handlers and prioritized kernel threads (`irq/<irq>-<name>`) scheduled under `SCHED_FIFO`.
4. *High-Resolution Timers (`hrtimers`)*: Traditional Linux timer ticks execute at coarse periodic jiffies ($1\text{ ms}$ or $4\text{ ms}$ granularity), introducing substantial quantization error and timer slack. `PREEMPT_RT` binds the timer subsystem to hardware per-CPU clock event devices (such as the ARM Generic Timer or x86 Local APIC), enabling sub-microsecond timer resolution. Real-time cyclic threads invoke `clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL)` using absolute monotonic deadlines, avoiding cumulative drift from relative sleeps. Wake-up jitter remains part of the response-time bound.

**Interrupt Handling Latency and Top-Half/Bottom-Half Partitioning.** When an external hardware peripheral (such as an IMU, joint encoder counter, or fieldbus controller) asserts an interrupt request (IRQ), the processor halts user execution, saves register context, and vectors to the hardware ISR via the interrupt controller (such as an ARM Generic Interrupt Controller GICv3 or x86 APIC). The worst-case interrupt latency $t_{\text{irq,lat}}$ to enter the hardware interrupt handler can be budgeted as:
$$ t_{\text{irq,lat}} = t_{\text{irq\_disabled,max}} + t_{\text{hw\_pipe}} + t_{\text{context\_save}} + \sum_{j \in hp(\text{irq})} t_{\text{ISR},j} $$
This expression does not include threaded-handler work or the subsequent scheduling delay before a user-space task runs. Here $t_{\text{irq\_disabled,max}}$ is the longest duration during which CPU interrupts were disabled across the kernel, $t_{\text{hw\_pipe}}$ is the processor pipeline flush delay, $t_{\text{context\_save}}$ is the hardware register preservation time, and $\sum t_{\text{ISR},j}$ represents the execution duration of higher-priority ISRs.

To prevent high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as GigE Vision cameras or 3D lidars streaming gigabits of packet traffic) from generating an *interrupt storm* that starves the 1 kHz permission path, real-time architectures strictly enforce top-half and bottom-half partitioning:

* **Top-half (Hardware ISR)**: Executes in hard-interrupt context with CPU interrupts masked. It executes the absolute minimum hardware operations—reading the peripheral interrupt status register, clearing the physical interrupt line, latching high-resolution hardware counter timestamps, and waking the associated threaded IRQ. The handler's maximum execution time must be bounded on the target.
* **Bottom-half (Threaded IRQ)**: In `PREEMPT_RT` and RTOS environments, complex packet deserialization, frame CRC verification, and data copies are deferred to dedicated kernel threads (`irq/<irq>-<name>`). By configuring these threaded IRQs under `SCHED_FIFO` with priorities lower than the 1 kHz safety monitor (e.g., setting camera IRQ threads to priority 50 and the motor permission thread to priority 90), the scheduler prevents those lower-priority threads from preempting the control task. Hard-interrupt top halves and shared-memory traffic still contribute interference.

**CPU Shielding, Core Isolation, and Cache Locality.** Heterogeneous multi-core robotics SoCs must isolate deterministic control threads from background operating-system disturbances. Kernel boot parameters establish strict CPU shielding:

* `isolcpus=2,3`: Removes cores 2 and 3 from the general kernel scheduler balancing domain, reducing automatic load balancing onto those cores; explicit affinity, cpusets, and kernel work still require configuration.
* `nohz_full=2,3`: Enables full dynamic tickless operation. When an isolated core runs a single real-time thread, the kernel can suppress the periodic scheduling timer tick ($100\text{--}1000\text{ Hz}$), removing that source of periodic interruption while other interrupts and scheduling delays remain.
* `rcu_nocbs=2,3`: Offloads RCU callback processing from isolated cores to housekeeping cores (cores 0 and 1).
* *IRQ Affinity Partitioning*: Peripheral hardware interrupts are directed away from real-time cores by writing CPU bitmasks to `/proc/irq/<id>/smp_affinity`. High-rate camera MSI-X vectors and Ethernet controller interrupts are pinned exclusively to housekeeping cores, reducing controllable interrupt interference. Nonmaskable events, local timers, and platform firmware disturbances still require accounting.
* *Cache Line Alignment and False Sharing Elimination*: Cache-line size is architecture dependent; the examples here assume 64-byte lines. When multiple CPU cores access independent variables that reside within the same 64-byte line, hardware cache coherency protocols (MESI/MOESI) repeatedly invalidate the line across core private caches upon every store—a phenomenon known as **false sharing** or *cache line bouncing*. A single false sharing interaction can stall a real-time core for 50 to 100 clock cycles. Separating independently written state into aligned, padded cache-line slots avoids false sharing; merely aligning the beginning of a larger structure does not isolate every member. The target's remaining cache misses and contention still need timing bounds. Furthermore, real-time control paths pre-warm L1 instruction and data caches during initialization by executing a dummy pass over critical control tables before arming actuators.

**Memory Locking, Allocation Invariants, and Page Fault Elimination.** Virtual memory subsystems rely on demand paging: when a process accesses an unmapped virtual address, the CPU raises an architectural page fault exception (`#PF`), suspending execution while the kernel page-table handler allocates a physical page frame, updates translation lookaside buffer (TLB) entries, and zeroes the memory (a *minor page fault*, requiring $10\text{--}50\,\mu\text{s}$). If the requested page was swapped to secondary flash storage, the thread blocks on disk I/O (a *major page fault*, requiring $10\text{--}50\text{ ms}$). Furthermore, Transparent Huge Pages (THP) memory compaction (`khugepaged`) can asynchronously stall threads for tens of milliseconds while defragmenting physical memory pages. A page fault can consume the remaining response-time margin; its mere occurrence does not imply that every deadline is missed.

The following Linux/glibc sketch illustrates initialization and absolute-period sleeping. It assumes the shown page and cache-line sizes. Production code must also validate limits and privileges, measure completion against the deadline, and enter the assessed fallback on an overrun. A late absolute sleep can return immediately; it must not trigger an uncontrolled series of catch-up actuator writes.

```c
// Real-time process initialization, memory locking, and cyclic execution
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <sched.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <malloc.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>

#define REALTIME_PRIORITY   90
#define CONTROL_CPU_CORE    2
#define STACK_PREFAULT_SZ   (256 * 1024)       // 256 KB stack
#define HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ    (16 * 1024 * 1024) // 16 MB pre-allocated arena
#define PERIOD_NS           1000000ULL         // 1 ms period (1 kHz)

// 64-byte cache-aligned telemetry slot to prevent false sharing
typedef struct __attribute__((aligned(64))) {
    uint64_t sequence_id;
    uint64_t timestamp_ns;
    float joint_torques[8];
    uint32_t status_flags;
    uint8_t reserved[12];
} realtime_telemetry_t;

static realtime_telemetry_t g_telemetry;
static volatile uint8_t *g_realtime_heap_arena = NULL;

void configure_realtime_process(int target_cpu, int rt_priority, size_t stack_size) {
    // 1. Bind execution to dedicated isolated CPU core (isolcpus / nohz_full)
    cpu_set_t cpuset;
    CPU_ZERO(&cpuset);
    CPU_SET(target_cpu, &cpuset);
    if (sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(cpu_set_t), &cpuset) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setaffinity failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 2. Configure POSIX static real-time priority (SCHED_FIFO)
    struct sched_param sp = { .sched_priority = rt_priority };
    if (sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, &sp) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setscheduler SCHED_FIFO failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 3. Lock all current and future virtual address mappings into physical RAM
    if (mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) != 0) {
        perror("mlockall failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 4. Disable glibc dynamic heap trimming and anonymous mmap allocation
    mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, -1);
    mallopt(M_MMAP_MAX, 0);

    // 5. Pre-allocate and prefault the dedicated heap arena
    g_realtime_heap_arena = (uint8_t *)malloc(HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ);
    if (!g_realtime_heap_arena) {
        perror("malloc heap arena failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    // Touch every 4 KB page to force physical page frame allocation and TLB population
    for (size_t i = 0; i < HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ; i += 4096) {
        g_realtime_heap_arena[i] = 0;
    }

    // 6. Prefault the thread execution stack to its declared maximum depth
    volatile char stack_buffer[stack_size];
    for (size_t i = 0; i < stack_size; i += 4096) {
        stack_buffer[i] = 0; // Trigger minor page fault and populate TLB entry
    }
}

void run_periodic_control_loop(void) {
    struct timespec next_period;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &next_period);

    // A real implementation warms the actual control code and data before arming.

    while (1) {
        // Compute next absolute wake epoch (eliminates cumulative drift)
        next_period.tv_nsec += PERIOD_NS;
        while (next_period.tv_nsec >= 1000000000L) {
            next_period.tv_nsec -= 1000000000L;
            next_period.tv_sec  += 1;
        }

        // High-resolution absolute sleep
        int ret;
        do {
            ret = clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL);
        } while (ret == EINTR);
        if (ret != 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "clock_nanosleep: %s\n", strerror(ret));
            break;
        }

        // ZERO-ALLOCATION CYCLIC CONTROL LOGIC
        // 1. Ingest sensor state from lock-free shared memory
        // 2. Evaluate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)
        // 3. Dispatch admitted setpoints to EtherCAT master
        g_telemetry.sequence_id++;
    }
}
```

Beyond address space locking and stack prefaulting, the cyclic 1 kHz control loop operates under a strict **zero dynamic allocation invariant**. In general-purpose systems programming, developers routinely rely on dynamic memory managers (`malloc`, `free`, C++ `new`, `delete`) or standard container expansions (`std::vector::push_back`). In a real-time control loop, however, dynamic allocation introduces three catastrophic failure modes:

1. *Arena Mutex Contention*: Modern allocators (such as `ptmalloc` in `glibc`) partition memory into multiple heap arenas protected by mutual-exclusion mutexes. If another thread in the same process acquires an arena lock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time control thread calling `malloc` blocks on that mutex, suffering from priority inversion and waiting milliseconds.
2. *Kernel Syscall Invocations*: When an allocator exhausts its active arena chunk, it issues `brk()` or anonymous `mmap()` system calls. These kernel entries acquire the process's `mmap_lock` (or `mmap_sem`), which is shared with background kernel threads such as `khugepaged` performing transparent huge page compaction or memory defragmentation, stalling user-space execution for tens of milliseconds.
3. *Heap Fragmentation*: Repeated cyclic allocations and deallocations fragment the heap, degrading allocation search times across segregated free lists into non-deterministic search loops.

Consequently, all message structures, matrix workspace buffers, trajectory buffers, and seqlock mailbox slots must be statically allocated at startup or drawn from fixed-size, lock-free memory pools (such as slab allocators). Furthermore, `mlockall(MCL_FUTURE)` must be paired with explicit memory pre-allocation and page prefaulting: Linux utilizes optimistic memory allocation (overcommit), meaning virtual address ranges returned by `malloc()` are not backed by physical page frames until the thread actually writes to each 4 KB page. Touching an uninitialized buffer for the first time inside the control loop triggers a minor page fault exception (`#PF`), which forces the kernel page-fault handler to allocate physical memory, zero the page, and update the MMU page table and TLB entries—a stall of $10\text{--}50\,\mu\text{s}$ that jeopardizes sub-millisecond control deadlines. Prefaulting and successful memory locking establish page residency before arming actuators. TLB and cache entries can still be evicted, so their miss costs remain in the execution budget; copy-on-write faults and later mapping changes must also be excluded.

### Hardware watchdogs and fault response

In distributed computing clusters, node liveness and consensus are managed via software heartbeats and distributed leases (such as Raft heartbeats, ZooKeeper leases, or Kubernetes node probes) operating over second-scale intervals. If a worker node crashes, the cluster orchestrator reschedules containers onto alternative nodes.

In physical AI systems, an autonomous machine traveling through physical space cannot wait seconds for a software orchestrator. If the GPU driver deadlocks, memory bus crossbars stall, or a kernel panic freezes the operating system, physical momentum continues unchecked. To detect a missed execution checkpoint, an embedded design uses a **hardware watchdog timer**.\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter}\index{Watchdog timer!windowed watchdog}\index{Watchdog timer!token-passing liveness} Its clock and response path must be independent of the monitored processor; an independent crystal oscillator or low-speed internal oscillator (`LSI`) completely decoupled from the main system phase-locked loop (PLL) is required.

**Hardware Down-Counters and Windowed Servicing.** The hardware watchdog timer comprises an autonomous down-counter register $W(t)$ clocked at frequency $f_{\text{wdg}}$ (typically $32\text{ kHz}$ from an independent on-chip RC oscillator). At system initialization, the register is loaded with a threshold value $W_{\text{init}}$. Software execution threads must periodically refresh (or "kick") the register before the count decrements to zero:
$$ W(t) = W_{\text{init}} - \left\lfloor f_{\text{wdg}} \cdot t \right\rfloor $$
At expiry, the timer asserts its configured reset or fault output; a separately wired trip is required when reset alone is insufficient.

In safety-critical systems, simple down-counters are vulnerable to runaway execution bugs: if a corrupted control loop enters an infinite spin-loop that happens to execute the watchdog refresh instruction, the watchdog is continually fed despite the control failure. To prevent this, robust physical AI architectures employ a **Windowed Watchdog Timer (WWDG)**. A windowed watchdog defines both an upper bound $W_{\text{upper}}$ and a lower bound $W_{\text{lower}}$. The software refresh is valid only within the admissible time window:
$$ W_{\text{lower}} \le W(t_k) \le W_{\text{upper}} $$
which defines an admissible servicing window $[t_{\text{win,open}}, t_{\text{win,close}}]$:
$$ t_{\text{win,open}} = \frac{W_{\text{init}} - W_{\text{upper}}}{f_{\text{wdg}}}, \quad t_{\text{win,close}} = \frac{W_{\text{init}} - W_{\text{lower}}}{f_{\text{wdg}}} $$
If software attempts to refresh the watchdog too early ($W(t_k) > W_{\text{upper}}$)—indicating an abnormal loop short-circuit or clock glitch—or fails to refresh before the configured closing threshold, the hardware watchdog controller trips immediately.

**Multi-Stage Token-Passing Liveness Checkpoints.** Feeding the watchdog directly from a periodic timer interrupt is an unsafe anti-pattern, because the timer interrupt may continue firing even if the primary motion planning and safety monitor threads are deadlocked. To check completion of the expected software checkpoints, control software can implement **token-passing checkpointing** using rolling polynomial accumulators:
$$ T_{k+1} = \text{CRC32}\left( T_k \oplus \text{Signature}_k \right) $$

1. At the beginning of the 1 kHz tick, an execution token $T_0$ is generated from the hardware monotonic cycle counter.
2. Stage 1 (Sensor Ingress): Validates camera, IMU, and joint telemetry timestamps, updating the token: $T_1 = \text{CRC32}(T_0 \oplus \text{sensor\_valid\_signature})$.
3. Stage 2 (State Estimation & Tracking): Computes joint tracking errors, updating $T_2 = \text{CRC32}(T_1 \oplus \text{tracking\_valid\_signature})$.
4. Stage 3 (Permission Enforcer): Validates Control Barrier Functions and stopping distance envelopes, computing $T_3 = \text{CRC32}(T_2 \oplus \text{enforce\_valid\_signature})$.
5. Stage 4 (Actuator Dispatch): Transmits admitted setpoints across the fieldbus, computing $T_{\text{final}} = \text{CRC32}(T_3 \oplus \text{dispatch\_valid\_signature})$.

Only if $T_{\text{final}}$ matches the expected value for this tick may the watchdog refresh routine service the timer. The token detects omitted or misordered checkpoints under its fault model; a CRC is neither authentication nor proof that the computed state or command is physically correct.

**Hardware Fail-Safe Interlocks and Safe Torque Off.** A watchdog timeout must reach a validated response path independently of the processor it monitors. A CPU reset or non-maskable interrupt alone does not establish that connection. When the assessed response includes safe torque off, a separately wired output disables the gate drive that generates motor torque; the wiring, response time, and diagnostic coverage require device-specific qualification.

Gate disable does not establish an instantaneous mechanical stop. Winding current takes time to decay, moving axes may coast, and a gravity-loaded axis may require a holding brake or a powered stop before torque removal. The complete watchdog-to-plant response belongs in the stopping budget.[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]

[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]: **Hardware Watchdog Down-Counters**\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter}: A configured watchdog expires when its expected service does not occur. Its oscillator, timeout, output wiring, and plant response differ by device. Feeding it merely from an unrelated interrupt does not prove that the monitored control computation progressed; a firmware-fed reset also need not signal a drive. See the [Linux watchdog API](https://docs.kernel.org/watchdog/watchdog-api.html) for reset behavior and @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder for stop selection.

## Inverter Timers and Power Electronics Gate Drive {#sec-appendix-systems-inverters}

In machine learning control frameworks (such as reinforcement learning policies, imitation learning, or model predictive control pipelines), actuator actions are formulated as continuous numerical setpoints—such as commanded joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}^*$ or angular velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}^*$. In physical realization, however, torque is generated by synthesizing rotating electromagnetic stator flux through high-frequency switching of power semiconductor bridges (typically at $20\text{ kHz}$ to $100\text{ kHz}$). Actuator motor drives employ three-phase half-bridge inverters to convert DC bus voltage into alternating stator currents.

### Microcontroller timer dead-time insertion

Bridging the digital software domain with physical power silicon requires strict microarchitectural timing interlocks. Each inverter phase comprises a half-bridge with a high-side power MOSFET (or GaN FET / IGBT) and a low-side power MOSFET connected across the DC supply rail $V_{\text{bus}}$. Microcontroller timer peripherals generate complementary pulse-width-modulated (PWM) drive signals with hardware-enforced **dead-time insertion** $t_{\text{dead}}$:\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}\index{Inverter!shoot-through protection}\index{Inverter!dead-time distortion}\index{Power MOSFET!Miller plateau dynamics}
$$ t_{\text{dead}} \ge t_{\text{off, max}} + t_{\text{prop, skew}} - t_{\text{on, min}} + t_{\text{margin}} $$
where $t_{\text{off, max}}$ is the maximum turn-off delay of the power switch, $t_{\text{on, min}}$ is the minimum turn-on delay, $t_{\text{prop, skew}}$ is the propagation delay mismatch across isolated gate drivers, and $t_{\text{margin}}$ is an engineering safety buffer.[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]

**Microcontroller Advanced Timer Architecture.** Modern motor control microcontrollers (such as STM32 Advanced-control timers TIM1/TIM8 or TI C2000 ePWM modules) synthesize PWM waveforms using hardware up-down counting counters (`TIMx_CNT`). In **center-aligned mode**, the counter counts up from 0 to the auto-reload value (`TIMx_ARR`) and back down to 0, producing symmetrical PWM waveforms with period $T_{\text{pwm}} = 2 \cdot \text{ARR} \cdot T_{\text{timer\_clk}}$. Center-aligned PWM provides symmetric switching and repeatable ADC trigger opportunities. Ripple reduction and valid sampling windows depend on duty cycle, modulation, current-sensing topology, and settling time; synchronization alone does not remove switching noise.

The timer's hardware Dead-Time Generator (DTG) monitors the compare match outputs (`TIMx_CCRx`) and inserts dead-time delay cycles $N_{\text{dtg}}$ using an autonomous digital delay line:
$$ t_{\text{dead}} = N_{\text{dtg}} \cdot T_{\text{dtg}} $$
By latching the DTG configuration behind hardware register lock bits (`BDTR.LOCK`), the microcontroller guarantees that the dead-time delay cannot be altered by runaway firmware or memory corruption.

**Gate Charge Dynamics and Asymmetric Switching.** A power MOSFET or GaN FET switch possesses input capacitance $C_{\text{iss}} = C_{\text{gs}} + C_{\text{gd}}$, where $C_{\text{gd}}$ is the non-linear reverse transfer (Miller) capacitance. During gate turn-on and turn-off, charge transfer follows:
$$ Q_g = \int_0^{t_{\text{sw}}} I_g(t) dt = Q_{\text{gs}} + Q_{\text{gd}} $$
During turn-off, the gate driver sinks current through gate resistance $R_{g,\text{off}}$. The gate-source voltage $V_{\text{gs}}$ drops to the **Miller plateau voltage** $V_{\text{plateau}}$, where it dwells while the drain-to-source voltage $V_{\text{ds}}$ traverses the entire DC rail:
$$ t_{\text{plateau}} = \frac{Q_{\text{gd}}}{I_{g,\text{off}}} = \frac{Q_{\text{gd}} \cdot R_{g,\text{off}}}{V_{\text{plateau}} - V_{\text{ee}}} $$
Turn-on and turn-off times depend on gate resistance, driver strength, load, and device charge. Neither is universally longer; dead time must use the measured worst-case mismatch.

**Shoot-Through Prevention and Parasitic Miller Turn-On.** If dead time is insufficient, both high-side and low-side switches conduct simultaneously, creating a low-impedance short circuit directly bridging the DC rail to ground:
$$ I_{\text{shoot-through}} = \frac{V_{\text{bus}}}{2 R_{\text{ds(on)}} + R_{\text{trace}}} $$
This resistive expression gives a prospective current, not its instantaneous value. Loop inductance limits the initial rise, and the resulting device stress depends on switching overlap, protection delay, and the circuit safe operating area.

Even when dead time is configured correctly, half-bridge legs face **parasitic Miller cross-conduction**. When the high-side MOSFET turns on, the phase node voltage slews at high speed ($dV_{\text{ds}}/dt \sim 10\text{--}50\text{ V/ns}$ in modern SiC and GaN bridges). This steep voltage transient forces displacement current through the low-side switch's Miller capacitance:
$$ I_{\text{miller}} = C_{\text{gd}} \frac{dV_{\text{ds}}}{dt} $$
This current flows through the low-side gate resistor $R_{g,\text{off}}$ back to ground, inducing a parasitic gate voltage rise:
$$ V_{\text{gs,induced}} = I_{\text{miller}} \cdot R_{g,\text{off}} = C_{\text{gd}} \frac{dV_{\text{ds}}}{dt} R_{g,\text{off}} $$
If $V_{\text{gs,induced}}$ exceeds the gate threshold voltage $V_{\text{th}}$ (typically $1.5\text{--}3.0\text{ V}$ in GaN FETs), the low-side switch turns on spuriously while the high-side switch is conducting, inducing catastrophic shoot-through. Power electronics gate drivers counter this using **Active Miller Clamps (AMC)**—an internal low-impedance switch that clamps the gate directly to the negative rail whenever $V_{\text{gs}}$ drops below $1.0\text{ V}$—or split gate drives ($R_{g,\text{on}} / R_{g,\text{off}}$) with antiparallel Schottky diodes.

**Dead-Time Voltage Distortion and Torque Ripple.** While necessary for silicon survival, dead time introduces non-linear voltage distortion into stator windings. During the dead-time interval $t_{\text{dead}}$, both active MOSFETs are commanded off, and phase current $I_{\text{phase}}$ is forced to freewheel through antiparallel body diodes. The sign of the phase current determines whether the inverter phase node clamps to $V_{\text{bus}}$ or ground, producing an average phase voltage error:
$$ \Delta V_{\text{phase}} = -\operatorname{sgn}(I_{\text{phase}}) \cdot \frac{t_{\text{dead}}}{T_{\text{pwm}}} V_{\text{bus}} $$
In three-phase synchronous machines, this square-wave error injects 5th and 7th harmonic voltages into the stationary reference frame. When transformed into the rotor synchronous $dq$ reference frame via Park's transformation, these odd harmonics combine into a **6th harmonic voltage disturbance**. The amplitudes and phases follow the harmonic coefficients of the phase-voltage error and the chosen transformation convention. They are not equal to the fundamental square-wave coefficient. The current loop filters these voltage harmonics before they become torque ripple.

This voltage distortion creates a corresponding **6th harmonic torque ripple**:
$$ \tau_{\text{ripple}}(6\theta_e) = \frac{3}{2} p \, \lambda_{\text{pm}} \cdot \Delta I_q(6\theta_e) $$
Left uncompensated, this hardware-induced torque ripple produces high-frequency torque chatter that excites mechanical drivetrain resonances. Modern motor drives implement dead-time compensation algorithms in low-level firmware that inject feedforward voltage vectors opposite to $\Delta V_{d,q}$, linearizing the actuator response for high-level ML policies.

[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]: **Inverter Dead-Time Insertion**\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}: Timer dead time is selected from switch and driver timing over temperature and load, then verified with the actual gate waveforms. An overlap can create a damaging bus short; a numeric current or fuse outcome requires the circuit impedance and protection response.

## Inductive Voltage Droop and Gate Delay Stretch {#sec-appendix-systems-droop}

In data center machine learning clusters, power delivery networks (PDNs) are supported by massive rack-level voltage regulator modules (VRMs) and extensive decoupling capacitor planes. On embedded Physical AI compute platforms, deep learning accelerators (such as tensor cores and systolic array matrix engines) share tightly constrained power rails with CPU cores and real-time safety microcontrollers. When a deep neural network transitions from idle to full execution, current draw increases by tens of amperes within nanoseconds.

### Power delivery network impedance and rail droop

A power delivery network (PDN) has parasitic resistance and inductance in each source path. For a lumped branch with resistance $R_{\text{PDN}}$, inductance $L_{\text{PDN}}$, and branch current $I_{\text{branch}}$, its voltage drop is:\index{Inductive voltage droop!power delivery network}\index{Power delivery network!target impedance}\index{Decoupling capacitors!multi-tier hierarchy}\index{Power delivery network!frequency-domain impedance}
$$ V_{\text{source}}-V_{\text{rail}} = L_{\text{PDN}} \frac{dI_{\text{branch}}}{dt} + I_{\text{branch}}R_{\text{PDN}} $$
The accelerator's load current need not equal this branch current during a transient: local decoupling supplies their difference. The rail response follows the coupled source-path and capacitor equations of @sec-appendix-systems-power. Substituting the full load-current slew into every upstream inductance would ignore that buffering.

**PDN Target Impedance Across Frequency Decades.** To prevent rail excursions from exceeding allowable voltage tolerances $\pm \Delta V_{\max} = V_{\text{nom}} \times \delta_{\text{tol}}$ (typically $\pm 5\text{ percent}$, or $45\text{ mV}$ on a $0.9\text{ V}$ digital core rail), the power delivery network must maintain an impedance profile strictly below the **target impedance** $Z_{\text{target}}$ across the entire operational frequency band:
$$ Z_{\text{target}} = \frac{V_{\text{nom}} \cdot \delta_{\text{tol}}}{\Delta I_{\max}} $$
For a $0.9\text{ V}$ accelerator drawing a $50\text{ A}$ step transient with $5\text{ percent}$ allowable ripple, $Z_{\text{target}} = 45\text{ mV} / 50\text{ A} = 0.90\text{ m}\Omega$ from DC up to gigahertz frequencies.

**Multi-Tier Decoupling Hierarchy.** Switched-mode power supplies (VRMs) have limited feedback control loop bandwidth ($100\text{ kHz}$ to $1\text{ MHz}$) and cannot supply charge during nanosecond current transitions. Energy must be buffered across a multi-tier decoupling capacitor hierarchy structured by frequency response:

1. *On-Die Decoupling ($> 100\text{ MHz}$)*: Deep trench and metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors fabricated directly on the silicon die ($C_{\text{die}} \sim 10\text{--}100\text{ nF}$, parasitic loop inductance $< 10\text{ pH}$, response time $< 0.5\text{ ns}$) supply charge during the initial clock cycles.
2. *Package Decoupling ($10\text{--}100\text{ MHz}$)*: Land-side capacitors (LSC) mounted under the BGA package ($C_{\text{pkg}} \sim 1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{F}$, loop inductance $\sim 50\text{--}200\text{ pH}$, response time $1\text{--}5\text{ ns}$).
3. *Board-Level High-Frequency MLCCs ($100\text{ kHz}\text{--}10\text{ MHz}$)*: Low-ESL surface-mount multi-layer ceramic capacitors (0201/0402 case sizes, $C \sim 0.1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{F}$, loop inductance $\sim 0.5\text{--}2\text{ nH}$, response time $10\text{--}100\text{ ns}$).
4. *Bulk Decoupling ($\text{DC}\text{--}100\text{ kHz}$)*: Polymer tantalum or aluminum electrolytic capacitors ($C_{\text{bulk}} \sim 100\text{--}1000\,\mu\text{F}$, response time $1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{s}$) sustain the rail until the active VRM regulation loop stabilizes.

**Anti-Resonance Voltage Spikes.** Parasitic inductance and parallel capacitor branches can create impedance peaks between their resonances. A simple LC frequency scale is $f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, but the peak magnitude requires the complete network, including capacitor equivalent series resistance and inductance. Excitation near a poorly damped peak can amplify supply excursions. A target-impedance check therefore needs the measured or modeled impedance spectrum, not capacitance alone.

### Digital logic gate delay and the alpha-power law

In sub-micron CMOS silicon, logic gate propagation delay $t_{\text{prop}}$ is governed by the Sakurai-Newton **alpha-power law**:[^fn-sys-sakurai-droop]
$$ t_{\text{prop}}(V) \propto \frac{C_L \cdot V}{(V - V_{\text{th}})^\alpha} $$
where $C_L$ is the gate load capacitance, $V_{\text{th}}$ is the transistor threshold voltage, and $\alpha \in [1.2, 1.5]$ is the velocity saturation index (contrasting with $\alpha = 2.0$ in long-channel theory).

When rail voltage droops from $V_{\text{nom}}$ to $V_{\text{droop}}$, propagation delay stretches according to:
